subject: biology
topicDisplay: D3–D4 — Continuity and change: organisms and ecosystems
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
What happens at fertilization in humans
Haploid gametes fuse to make a diploid zygote
Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
Natural selection: the mechanism, and the paradigm shift it caused
Ecosystems can stay the same kind of place for millions of years
What humans have added to the atmosphere
Boreal forest: from carbon sink to carbon source

questions.q: Aphids reproduce asexually through the summer, when conditions are stable and food is plentiful, and switch to sexual reproduction in autumn before conditions change. Which statement best explains this pattern?
options: Sexual reproduction is used in autumn because varied offspring are invariably fitter; the summer clones are a poor substitute produced under time pressure.
Summer clones copy an adapted genotype quickly; autumn sexual reproduction produces varied offspring for the changed conditions ahead.
Sexual reproduction is used in autumn so that the offspring gain the specific cold-tolerance features that the coming winter demands.
Asexual reproduction in summer shows that aphids are simple organisms; the autumn sexual stage is their true form of reproduction.
optionWhy: A student who believes variation is always an advantage picks this. In stable summer conditions the clones are the better strategy: every offspring inherits the whole adapted genotype.

Asexual reproduction suits an individual already adapted to the existing environment, giving many identical offspring fast. Sexual reproduction produces new gene combinations, the variation needed for adaptation to a changed environment.
A student who thinks variation is directed towards what is needed picks this. New allele combinations are random; some may happen to suit winter, and selection then favours those.

A student who files asexual reproduction with bacteria and simple organisms picks this. Many eukaryotes, including these insects, use both modes; the choice depends on the environment, not on complexity.
questions.explain: Asexual reproduction suits an individual already adapted to the existing environment, giving many identical offspring fast. Sexual reproduction produces new gene combinations, the variation needed for adaptation to a changed environment.

questions.q: A mutation in mitochondrial DNA is passed from a mother to all her children but is never passed on by a father. Which feature of fertilization explains this?
options: Sperm mitochondria enter the egg but are so outnumbered by the egg's own that their DNA is diluted away.
Each parent hands over exactly half of its DNA, and the mitochondrial DNA happens to fall in the mother's half.
The egg is larger because it carries more genetic material, including all the mitochondria required.
The sperm's mitochondria are destroyed after its nucleus has entered the egg cytoplasm.
optionWhy: A student who believes the sperm's mitochondria get in picks this. They do not enter: they are destroyed with the tail, so no paternal mitochondrial DNA is present to be diluted.

A student who pictures inheritance as each parent handing over a fixed half of its DNA picks this. Meiosis halves the nuclear DNA only; mitochondrial DNA is not part of that division, and the father passes on none because the sperm's mitochondria are destroyed at fertilization.

A student who equates the egg's size with extra genetic material picks this. The egg's size is due to food reserves; maternal inheritance of mitochondria is due to the fate of the sperm's mitochondria.
Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed. All the zygote's mitochondria, and so all its mitochondrial DNA, come from the egg.
questions.explain: Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed. All the zygote's mitochondria, and so all its mitochondrial DNA, come from the egg.

questions.q: Garden pea flowers pollinate and fertilize themselves before they open. Which statement about reproduction in the pea is correct?
options: It is asexual, because only one parent plant takes part in the process.
Fertilization is complete as soon as the pollen has landed on the flower's stigma.
It is sexual, because meiosis makes the gametes and they fuse at fertilization.
The pollen grains, being the male gametes, fuse directly with the ovules in the ovary.
optionWhy: A student who defines asexual reproduction by the number of parents picks this. The pea's gametes are made by meiosis and fuse, so its reproduction is sexual even though it self-fertilizes.
A student who equates pollination with fertilization picks this. After pollination a pollen tube must grow down the style before a male gamete can fuse with the female gamete.

Reproduction in flowering plants is sexual even if a plant is hermaphroditic: gametes formed by meiosis fuse to give a zygote. Whether the offspring differ from the parent depends on how heterozygous it is; what makes the process sexual is meiosis and fusion of gametes, not the number of parents.
A student who treats pollen as the gamete picks this. The pollen grain grows a tube that delivers the male gametes it contains to the female gamete inside the ovule.
questions.explain: Reproduction in flowering plants is sexual even if a plant is hermaphroditic: gametes formed by meiosis fuse to give a zygote. Whether the offspring differ from the parent depends on how heterozygous it is; what makes the process sexual is meiosis and fusion of gametes, not the number of parents.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the means of inheritance in eukaryotes that have a sexual life cycle?
options: Each parent produces haploid gametes by meiosis, and their fusion forms a diploid zygote with two copies of each autosomal gene
Each parent's gametes carry both of its alleles of every gene, so the zygote's traits blend the two parental genotypes
Haploid gametes fusing to form a zygote is the pattern in animals, while plants pass on their genes through pollen and seeds instead
Each gamete carries the parent's single copy of each gene, so the zygote formed at fertilization has one copy of each gene
optionWhy: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that each gamete carries one copy of each autosomal gene; fertilization restores the diploid number, giving the zygote two copies, one from each parent. This pattern is common to all sexually reproducing eukaryotes.

A student who thinks a parent passes on its whole genotype picks this. Gametes are haploid and carry only one allele of each gene, chosen at random in meiosis, and the alleles remain separate in the zygote rather than blending.

A student who files plant reproduction as a separate process picks this. Pollen contains male gametes and the ovule contains the female gamete; their fusion forms a diploid zygote, so plants follow the same haploid–diploid pattern as animals.

A student who pictures a gene as a single object in the cell picks this. A diploid parent has two copies of each autosomal gene and puts one into each gamete; the zygote therefore has two copies, one on each homologous chromosome.
questions.explain: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that each gamete carries one copy of each autosomal gene; fertilization restores the diploid number, giving the zygote two copies, one from each parent. This pattern is common to all sexually reproducing eukaryotes.

questions.q: A man and a woman are both unaffected carriers of the PKU allele. They already have one child with PKU. What is the probability that their next child will have PKU?
optionWhy: A student who treats the 2 in 4 heterozygous carriers as the children who 'have' PKU picks this. Carriers are unaffected, because one functional allele produces enough enzyme; only the 1 in 4 homozygous recessive (pp) children have PKU.

A student who believes PKU is caused by a dominant allele expects three quarters of the children of two heterozygotes to be affected. PKU is recessive, so only the homozygous recessive quarter is affected.

A student who reads a 3:1 ratio as a quota picks this, thinking the family has already had its one affected child in four. Each fertilization is independent; the probability is 1 in 4 for every child regardless of earlier children.

Both parents are heterozygous (Pp × Pp). The Punnett grid gives PP, Pp, pP and pp, so each fertilization has a 1 in 4 chance of producing a homozygous recessive child with PKU. Each child is an independent event, so the earlier affected child makes no difference.
questions.explain: Both parents are heterozygous (Pp × Pp). The Punnett grid gives PP, Pp, pP and pp, so each fertilization has a 1 in 4 chance of producing a homozygous recessive child with PKU. Each child is an independent event, so the earlier affected child makes no difference.

questions.q: A woman with blood group A whose genotype is IAi has children with a man of blood group B whose genotype is IBi. Which blood groups are possible in their children, and with what probabilities?
options: Groups A, B and AB, each 1 in 3, but not group O, as neither parent is group O
Groups AB, A, B and O are all possible, each with a probability of 1 in 4
Groups A and AB only, each 1 in 2, because the IA allele is dominant to IB
Groups A and B only, each 1 in 2, since each parent passes on its own group's allele
optionWhy: A student who thinks a child's blood group must match a parent's picks this. Both parents carry the recessive allele i, and an ii child, group O, is produced in 1 in 4 fertilizations.

The Punnett grid for IAi × IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), one cell each. IA and IB are codominant and both dominant to i, so all four ABO groups are possible with equal probability.
A student who forces the three alleles into a dominant/recessive hierarchy picks this. IA and IB are codominant, so IAIB is group AB, and IBi is group B; the option also ignores the ii children.

A student who treats blood group as a unit trait that a child takes from one parent or the other picks this. Each parent is heterozygous and passes on either of its two alleles with equal probability, so four genotypes, IAIB, IAi, IBi and ii, are possible, giving all four blood groups.
questions.explain: The Punnett grid for IAi × IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), one cell each. IA and IB are codominant and both dominant to i, so all four ABO groups are possible with equal probability.

questions.q: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia (XHXh) has children with a man who does not have haemophilia (XHY). Their first child is a boy. What is the probability that he has haemophilia?
optionWhy: A student who takes the 1 in 4 from the whole Punnett grid (XHXH, XHXh, XHY, XhY) and applies it to a son picks this. Among sons only, the two possibilities are XHY and XhY, so the probability is 1 in 2.
A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X from his mother. The mother passes XH or Xh with equal probability, so half of sons on average are XhY and have haemophilia.

A student who believes a carrier mother passes the condition to all of her sons picks this. She has one XH and one Xh and passes either with equal probability, so only half of her sons are expected to be affected.

A student who thinks haemophilia passes from father to son, and notes that this father is unaffected, picks this. A son inherits his X chromosome from his mother, so a carrier mother can have affected sons whatever the father's genotype.
questions.explain: A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X from his mother. The mother passes XH or Xh with equal probability, so half of sons on average are XhY and have haemophilia.

questions.q: The heights in centimetres of nine students are: 150, 152, 152, 155, 158, 160, 163, 170 and 175. What are the mean, median and mode of these heights?
options: Mean 158 cm, median 159.4 cm, and mode 152 cm
Mean of 159.4 cm, median 152 cm, mode 158 cm
Mean 158.6 cm, with median 158 cm and mode 152 cm
Mean 159.4 cm, median 158 cm, mode 152 cm
optionWhy: A student who thinks the median is the calculated average and the mean is the middle value swaps the two. The mean is the sum divided by the number of values, 159.4; the median is the middle value in order, 158.

A student who takes the mode to be the middle value and the median to be the most frequent value swaps those two. The median is the middle value, 158; the mode is the value that occurs most often, 152.

A student who treats the highest and lowest values as outliers and discards both before calculating picks this: (1435 − 175 − 150) / 7 = 158.6. A value is an outlier only if it lies more than 1.5 × IQR beyond a quartile; by that rule none of these nine values is an outlier, and the mean of the full data set is 159.4 cm.

The nine values sum to 1435, and 1435 / 9 = 159.4 (to one decimal place). The values are already in order, so the median is the fifth value, 158. The only value that appears twice is 152, so it is the mode.
questions.explain: The nine values sum to 1435, and 1435 / 9 = 159.4 (to one decimal place). The values are already in order, so the median is the fifth value, 158. The only value that appears twice is 152, so it is the mode.

questions.q: During a long run, a person's blood glucose concentration falls to 3.5 mmol L−1. Glucagon secretion increases and the concentration returns to 5 mmol L−1. Which description of this sequence is correct?
options: Positive feedback, because the response raised the variable, not lowered it.
Positive feedback, because the response was beneficial and restored health.
A breakdown of homeostasis, because glucose left its set point of 5 mmol L−1.
Negative feedback correcting a fall of the variable below its set point.
optionWhy: A student who thinks negative feedback can only lower a variable picks this. The direction that matters is relative to the deviation: the fall was reversed, so the feedback is negative.
A student who reads 'positive' as beneficial picks this. Positive feedback means a response that increases the original change; a beneficial correction that reverses a change is negative feedback.

A student who expects a regulated variable to stay fixed picks this. A deviation followed by a corrective return is homeostasis working, not failing; variables must move away from the set point before feedback can act.

The variable dropped below its set point and the response (glucagon) raised it back. Because the response opposed the change, this is negative feedback; it operates from below the set point just as insulin operates from above it.
questions.explain: The variable dropped below its set point and the response (glucagon) raised it back. Because the response opposed the change, this is negative feedback; it operates from below the set point just as insulin operates from above it.

questions.q: A person moves to a cold climate. After several weeks their resting metabolic rate has risen and they produce more heat even when not shivering. Which explanation is correct?
options: The pituitary gland is secreting thyroxin, which acts as quickly as a nerve impulse.
The hypothalamus has started to produce extra heat itself as the blood cools.
A thicker layer of white fat is making extra ATP, and the ATP is released as heat.
More thyroxin is being secreted, raising the rate of cell respiration.
optionWhy: A student who has merged the gland sequence and time scale picks this. The pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone; thyroxin comes from the thyroid gland, and its effect on metabolic rate develops over days, not seconds.

A student who thinks the control centre is also the heater picks this. The hypothalamus coordinates responses; the extra heat comes from the raised respiration of body tissues under the influence of thyroxin.

A student who confuses insulating white fat with heat-generating brown fat, and who thinks heat comes from ATP, picks this. White adipose tissue insulates; the raised metabolic rate here comes from thyroxin.

Prolonged cold exposure increases signalling from the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland, which stimulates the thyroid gland to secrete more thyroxin. Thyroxin raises the metabolic rate of most cells, so more heat is released; this hormonal response builds up over days, unlike shivering.
questions.explain: Prolonged cold exposure increases signalling from the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland, which stimulates the thyroid gland to secrete more thyroxin. Thyroxin raises the metabolic rate of most cells, so more heat is released; this hormonal response builds up over days, unlike shivering.

questions.q: Which statement about natural selection as the mechanism of evolutionary change is correct?
options: It produced the species that exist today and has now stopped acting upon any of them
It has operated continuously over billions of years and is still operating today
It causes the mutations that individuals need to survive new conditions
It acts to improve each species as a whole rather than on individual organisms
optionWhy: A student who files natural selection under history picks this. Selection pressures still operate on every population; the evolution of antibiotic resistance is a present-day example.

Natural selection operates wherever there is heritable variation, overproduction and a selection pressure. It has acted continuously over billions of years to produce the biodiversity of life on Earth and continues in every population now.
A student who thinks organisms produce the alleles they need picks this. Mutation is random and precedes selection; natural selection changes the frequencies of alleles that already exist.

A student who takes the species as the unit of selection picks this. Natural selection acts on differences between individuals in survival and reproduction; alleles spread because they raise the fitness of the individuals carrying them.
questions.explain: Natural selection operates wherever there is heritable variation, overproduction and a selection pressure. It has acted continuously over billions of years to produce the biodiversity of life on Earth and continues in every population now.

questions.q: In elephant seals, males fight for control of a stretch of beach, and the largest males mate with most of the females there. Which statement about the evolution of large body size in male elephant seals is correct?
options: Large males have the higher fitness simply because they are stronger, whether or not they succeed in mating
Large size is favoured by sexual selection because it increases a male's success in competing for mates
Fighting for mates is not a selection pressure, since only survival differences drive evolution
Large size evolved because it benefits the species by ensuring only the best genes are passed on
optionWhy: A student who uses the everyday meaning of fitness picks this. Fitness is reproductive potential; large size raises fitness here only because it leads to more offspring.

Sexual selection is a selection pressure arising from differences in mating success. Large males win fights, mate with more females and leave more offspring, so alleles for large size have increased in frequency in males.
A student who thinks selection is only about survival picks this. Differences in reproductive success change allele frequencies just as differences in survival do.

A student who thinks selection works for the good of the species picks this. Alleles for large size spread because they raise the fitness of the individual males carrying them, not for any benefit to the species.
questions.explain: Sexual selection is a selection pressure arising from differences in mating success. Large males win fights, mate with more females and leave more offspring, so alleles for large size have increased in frequency in males.

questions.q: Sediment cores from a desert basin contain pollen in every layer. The layers have been dated to span the last 30 million years, and the deepest layers contain pollen of the same drought-adapted plant families as the surface layers. What is the best conclusion from this evidence?
options: The region cannot have supported a stable ecosystem for so long, because a desert is too harsh to persist for millions of years.
A desert ecosystem has persisted in this region for tens of millions of years, so it has shown long-term stability.
The plants whose pollen is in the deepest layers must still be alive today for the ecosystem to count as stable.
The ecosystem was not stable, because the numbers of each species must have varied over 30 million years.
optionWhy: A student who thinks only productive ecosystems can be stable picks this. The evidence shows precisely that the desert did persist; harshness of conditions does not prevent continuity.

The same type of community, identified from its pollen, is present throughout 30 million years of dated sediment. That is direct evidence of an ecosystem persisting over a very long period, which is what stability means.

A student who thinks persistence must be shown by living individuals picks this. No plant lives for 30 million years; continuity of the community type, not survival of individuals, is the evidence of stability.
A student who equates stability with constant populations picks this. Population sizes fluctuate in every ecosystem; the persistence of the same kind of community is what shows stability.
questions.explain: The same type of community, identified from its pollen, is present throughout 30 million years of dated sediment. That is direct evidence of an ecosystem persisting over a very long period, which is what stability means.

questions.q: A class plans to use mesocosms to investigate the effect of light intensity on ecosystem stability. Which design is most likely to succeed and to follow IB experimental guidelines?
options: Sealed glass jars containing pond water, algae, small aquatic invertebrates and sediment, placed at different distances from a lamp for several weeks.
Open terraria containing soil, plants and a small lizard, placed at different distances from a lamp, since a terrestrial model is more realistic.
Open tanks of pond water and algae with an air pump running in each, so that the organisms do not run out of oxygen during the investigation.
A single large sealed aquarium containing fish, because a bigger and more realistic model gives results that apply directly to real lakes.
optionWhy: Aquatic mesocosms are more likely to be successful than terrestrial ones, sealing prevents exchange of matter while light still enters, and small invertebrates in pond water can be kept without causing suffering, in line with IB guidelines.

A student who equates realism with size and animals picks this. Terrestrial mesocosms are less likely to succeed, and exposing a vertebrate to treatments that may harm it does not follow IB experimental guidelines.

A student who thinks oxygen must be supplied from outside picks this. Photosynthesis by the algae supplies the oxygen; an open, aerated tank allows matter to enter and leave, so it no longer tests whether the system can sustain itself.

A student who thinks a model reproduces reality exactly picks this. One vessel cannot test the effect of a variable, and no mesocosm, however large, gives results that transfer directly to a natural lake.
questions.explain: Aquatic mesocosms are more likely to be successful than terrestrial ones, sealing prevents exchange of matter while light still enters, and small invertebrates in pond water can be kept without causing suffering, in line with IB guidelines.

questions.q: Records for a cod fishery show that the annual catch stayed close to 250 000 tonnes for 20 years. Over the same period the number of fishing days needed to land that catch doubled, and the mean age of the cod caught fell from 8 years to 4 years. What do these data indicate?
options: Harvesting is sustainable, because the catch has remained constant for two decades and so the stock must be replacing itself.
Harvesting is sustainable, because cod are a renewable resource that reproduce each year and so cannot be depleted by fishing.
The fall in the mean age of the catch cannot affect replacement, because the reproductive rate of any species is a fixed value.
The stock is being harvested unsustainably: more effort is needed for the same catch and few fish now survive to old age.
optionWhy: A student who judges sustainability from the catch alone picks this. The catch has been maintained only by doubling effort and by taking younger fish, which are signs of a declining stock.

A student who thinks renewable means inexhaustible picks this. A renewable resource is depleted whenever the rate of harvesting exceeds the rate of replacement, and the effort and age data show this is happening.

A student who thinks replacement rate is fixed picks this. Replacement depends on the number of mature fish left to breed; removing fish at younger ages reduces the breeding stock and so reduces replacement.

A constant catch obtained with doubled effort means catch per unit effort has halved, so the stock has declined. A falling mean age shows that fish are being removed before they grow old, reducing the breeding stock. Both indicate harvesting above the replacement rate.
questions.explain: A constant catch obtained with doubled effort means catch per unit effort has halved, so the stock has declined. A falling mean age shows that fish are being removed before they grow old, reducing the breeding stock. Both indicate harvesting above the replacement rate.

questions.q: A farm sprays insecticide and herbicide several times each season. Downstream, insect and amphibian numbers have fallen and residues of the sprays are found in well water. Which factor affecting the sustainability of agriculture do these observations illustrate?
options: Supply of inputs, since the sprays are inputs that protect the crop yield and so make the farm more sustainable.
Pollution due to agrochemicals, since the sprays have harmed non-target organisms and contaminated water beyond the farm.
Leaching of nutrients, since sprays act only on pests within the field, so the downstream losses must be due to fertilizer.
Carbon footprint, since the only effect of agrochemicals beyond the field is from the fuel burned by the machinery that sprays them.
optionWhy: A student who sees inputs only as benefits picks this. Supply of inputs is a sustainability factor because producing and applying them has costs; here the observations show damage caused by the inputs, which is pollution due to agrochemicals.

Insecticides and herbicides are agrochemicals. The fall in downstream insects and amphibians and the residues in well water show that the sprays have harmed non-target organisms and polluted water off the farm, which is the pollution factor the guide lists.

A student who thinks pesticides act only on the target pests within the field picks this. No fertilizer is mentioned; the residues in the well water are from the sprays, and insecticides and herbicides kill many non-target species when they drift, run off or leach from the field.

A student who thinks the impact of agrochemicals is only the fuel used to apply them picks this. Carbon footprint concerns greenhouse gas emissions; the observations describe toxic effects on organisms and contamination of water, which is pollution due to agrochemicals.
questions.explain: Insecticides and herbicides are agrochemicals. The fall in downstream insects and amphibians and the residues in well water show that the sprays have harmed non-target organisms and polluted water off the farm, which is the pollution factor the guide lists.

questions.q: In a study of an estuary, DDT concentrations were measured in parts per million (ppm): water 0.00005, plankton 0.04, small fish 0.5, larger predatory fish 2, fish-eating birds 25. Which statement explains this pattern?
options: DDT is fat-soluble and not excreted, so each consumer retains the DDT from all its prey and the concentration rises at each trophic level.
Birds live longer than fish, so the pattern is due only to each bird having had more years in which to accumulate DDT.
Each organism absorbed DDT directly from the water, so the birds must have been exposed to more contaminated water.
Birds at the top of the food chain eat the greatest mass of food, so they take in the largest total amount of DDT.
optionWhy: This is biomagnification. The toxin taken in with every prey item is retained in fatty tissue, so a consumer's tissues hold a higher concentration than its food; over four trophic levels the concentration rose about half a million times above that in the water.

A student who confuses biomagnification with accumulation over a lifetime picks this. Longevity contributes, but the step-up occurs at every trophic level, including from plankton to short-lived small fish.
A student who thinks pollutants are taken up only from the surroundings picks this. All these organisms live in or beside the same water; the difference comes from DDT concentrated in food.

A student who confuses total intake with concentration picks this. Eating a large mass of prey is not itself the explanation; the concentration is high because the DDT from all the prey eaten is retained in a much smaller mass of bird tissue, and this step-up occurs at every trophic level.
questions.explain: This is biomagnification. The toxin taken in with every prey item is retained in fatty tissue, so a consumer's tissues hold a higher concentration than its food; over four trophic levels the concentration rose about half a million times above that in the water.

questions.q: Antarctic ice cores show that, over the last 800 000 years, periods of high global temperature coincided with high atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations and periods of low temperature with low concentrations. Which statement about this evidence is correct?
options: It shows a positive correlation, but the causal link between carbon dioxide and temperature is established by other evidence.
It shows a positive correlation, which by itself proves that carbon dioxide raises global temperatures.
It shows a negative correlation in cold periods, when both variables fell, and a positive one in warm periods.
It shows a correlation, but the warming was caused by thinning of the ozone layer rather than by carbon dioxide.
optionWhy: The ice-core data show a positive correlation over hundreds of thousands of years. A correlation does not prove causation; the causal link is confirmed by other evidence, such as the measured absorption of infrared radiation by carbon dioxide.

A student who takes a strong correlation as proof of cause picks this. Correlation alone cannot prove causation, since both variables could respond to a third factor; the causal link needs other evidence.

A student who thinks the sign of a correlation describes whether the variables are rising or falling picks this. High goes with high and low with low throughout, which is a single positive correlation.
A student who merges ozone depletion with global warming picks this. Ozone depletion is a separate problem; the causal link between carbon dioxide and warming is established by other evidence.
questions.explain: The ice-core data show a positive correlation over hundreds of thousands of years. A correlation does not prove causation; the causal link is confirmed by other evidence, such as the measured absorption of infrared radiation by carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Researchers measured the carbon in the soil organic layer of a boreal forest after fires. In stands older than 70 years, the carbon that remained was older than the trees and had survived earlier fires. In stands younger than 60 years on drier sites, the fire had burnt through this old carbon. What do these results show?
options: Fires release only carbon fixed since the previous fire, so regrowth of the trees will restore the carbon balance.
The forest has crossed a tipping point, so its carbon stock will recover gradually once the fires are out.
The old carbon lost from the young stands was ancient gas trapped in frozen soil that escaped as it thawed.
Fires in young stands on dry sites combust legacy carbon that older stands protect from burning.
optionWhy: A student who thinks fires are carbon neutral picks this. In the young stands the fire burnt carbon older than the trees, so it released carbon that regrowth cannot replace before the next fire.
A student who thinks a tipping point is followed by gradual recovery picks this. A tipping point marks a shift to a new state, net carbon loss, which may not be reversible.
A student who pictures trapped gas picks this. The old carbon was stored organic matter in the soil organic layer that was combusted by the fire, not gas released by thawing.

Legacy carbon is carbon in the soil organic layer that survived previous fires. In older stands a thick organic layer protected it, but in young stands on dry sites the fire burnt into it, releasing carbon stored over many fire cycles.
questions.explain: Legacy carbon is carbon in the soil organic layer that survived previous fires. In older stands a thick organic layer protected it, but in young stands on dry sites the fire burnt into it, releasing carbon stored over many fire cycles.

questions.q: The bird species of a mountain in New Guinea were surveyed in 1965 and again in 2012. For most species both the upper and the lower limits of the altitudinal range had moved upslope, by about 100 m on average, over a period in which the region warmed. What is the best interpretation?
options: The species have expanded their ranges, since they now occupy about 100 m more of the mountain.
Because both limits moved equally, the species have lost none of their habitat area.
The correlation between warming and the shift proves that no other factor was involved.
The ranges of the species shifted upslope, tracking the rise in temperature.
optionWhy: A student who equates a range shift with expansion picks this. Both limits moved up by a similar amount, so the range moved rather than growing.

A student who thinks a range shift is cost-free picks this. A mountain narrows towards its summit, so a band of the same height contains less area higher up, and species near the top have nowhere left to go.
A student who treats a correlation as proof of cause picks this. The pattern is consistent with warming, but a correlation alone cannot rule out other factors.

Both range limits moving upslope as the region warmed is the pattern expected when a species tracks the band of temperatures it can tolerate. Upslope shifts of montane birds in New Guinea are evidence of range shifts driven by climate change.
questions.explain: Both range limits moving upslope as the region warmed is the pattern expected when a species tracks the band of temperatures it can tolerate. Upslope shifts of montane birds in New Guinea are evidence of range shifts driven by climate change.
